hints: Look closely at statement 1 and think about specificity. Does one B-lymphocyte make many different antibodies, or is it locked to just one shape?
Recall what happens after clonal selection: which cells become memory cells, what plasma cells do, and what helper T-lymphocytes do to phagocytes.
walkthrough:
**Test Statement 1 - One B-cell, One Antibody**

Think of clonal selection. Each B-lymphocyte has receptors for one specific antigen only.

When activated, it divides to make plasma cells that secrete that one type of antibody. So statement 1 is false, it cannot make several types.

**Test Statements 2 and 3 - Memory and Plasma Cells**

After activation, some B-lymphocytes and some T-lymphocytes do not fight now. They become long-lived memory cells for a faster secondary response. So statement 2 is true.

Activated B-lymphocytes also form plasma cells, which are antibody factories that release large amounts of antibody into the blood plasma. So statement 3 is true.

**Test Statement 4 - T-cells Help Phagocytes**

Some T-lymphocytes are helper T-cells. They release cytokines that stimulate macrophages to carry out phagocytosis more vigorously to destroy infected cells. So statement 4 is true.

True statements are 2, 3 and 4 only, which is option D.

options.A: Incorrect because it includes statement 1, which is false. Each B-lymphocyte is specific and makes only one type of antibody.
options.B: Incorrect because it includes statement 1 and leaves out statement 4. Statement 1 is false and statement 4 is true.
options.C: Incorrect because it includes false statement 1 and leaves out true statements 2 and 3.
options.D: Correct because statements 2, 3 and 4 are all true, while statement 1 is false.
